Abstract
Future fighter operations are expected to combine increasingly capable autonomy, collaborative aircraft, dense sensor information, and sustained physiological and cognitive demands. This Perspective proposes a pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework in which the pilot, a pilot-specific digital twin, an intelligent flight-management system, the aircraft, and external agents are treated as interdependent elements within a systems-of-systems framework. The framework does not replace situation awareness, distributed cognition, joint cognitive systems, adaptive automation, or human-autonomy teaming. Instead, it extends their unit of analysis by making the pilot’s dynamic physiological and neurocognitive state, longitudinal variability, and health-related constraints explicit system variables and design objectives. The pilot digital twin is defined narrowly as an individualized state-estimation and forecasting capability, whereas the intelligent flight-management system integrates pilot, platform, mission, and environmental information to provide explainable recommendations and, where authorized, bounded adaptive action. We identify testable propositions concerning individualized prediction, adaptive support, shared situation awareness, trust calibration, and governance. The framework is prospective and requires validation in simulation, training, and operationally representative environments. Its purpose is to organize research toward systems that protect pilot agency, sustain performance, and preserve long-term health while exploiting increasingly a

sight. These safeguards are not peripheral constraints; they are conditions for trustworthiness and sustained adoption.
8. Limitations
This Perspective is intentionally forward-looking and does not validate a specific aircraft architecture, sensing suite, digital-twin implementation, or autonomy policy. Public descriptions of developmental military systems are incomplete and should not be treated as authoritative evidence of final capability. The term future fighter is therefore used instead of assigning the framework to a specific numbered generation.
Ecology is presently an organizing ontology and research heuristic, not a mathematically specified predictive theory. Its value will depend on whether the proposed entities, relationships, and propositions can be operationalized and tested. Several components may also be distributed across software and hardware rather than implemented as discrete modules. The PDT-IFMS separation is functional, not necessarily physical.
Finally, physiological inference in operational aviation remains constrained by signal quality, movement, environmental artifact, individual variability, construct ambiguity, and limited ground truth. A technologically sophisticated model can still be unsafe if it estimates the wrong construct, communicates certainty poorly, or triggers an ineffective response. The framework should therefore be treated as a research agenda, not an endorsement of immediate operational deployment.
9. Discussion
Future fighter aviation may evolve from interaction between a pilot and a collection of tools toward coordination within a distributed human-autonomy system. Established human-factors theories already explain many essential features of this transition. The pilot-wellness-informed ecological framework proposed here integrates those foundations with individualized physiological modeling, digital twins, adaptive autonomy, and longitudinal health considerations.
The central design principle is functional clarity. The PDT estimates and forecasts pilot state; the IFMS integrates pilot, platform, mission, and external information; the pilot retains intent, authorization, and override; and the aircraft executes commands within certified constraints. Pilot wellness becomes both an input to adaptation and an outcome by which the joint system is judged. The framework is deliberately testable and bounded by uncertainty, human authority, privacy, cybersecurity, and certification. Its success should be measured not by how much autonomy is added, but by whether the resulting team is safer, more predictable, more resilient, and better able to preserve pilot performance and long-term health.

The author acknowledges the professional experience and discussions that motivated the original exploratory concept, including pilot digital-twin research undertaken during 2022–2024, and thanks colleagues who encouraged development of the Perspective and provided critical feedback.
